newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Copper surplus coming...or it should be.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Copper surplus coming...or it should be.

text.p: Copper's arithmetic turned out to be as volatile as its price in 1996.
With the Sumitomo Corp scandal slipping into traders' history books, red metal minds are once more furiously number crunching to see if or when that elusive surplus will hit the market.
Their record is not encouraging so far.
Most analysts kicked off the year predicting a big surplus by Christmas.
LME stocks have just edged off a six-year low.
And World Bureau of Metal Statistics data showed half a million tonnes of copper lurking in Rotterdam.
Dutch customs officers were later sent to the back of the class for adding wrongly.
Worryingly, Holland's hoax came after initial steps were taken earlier in the year to improve the speed and quality of globally gathered copper data.

"All the expectations that a surplus was going to build up in the second half of this year did not happen, and we are probably going to end up being about in balance," said analyst Robert Lesemann of CRU International.
Delays and glitches bedevilled a string of new copper projects, gouging 100,000 to 150,000 tonnes of production from initial forecasts, Lesemann estimated.
"But the inevitable build up of stocks will take place and we are going to see the market coming off over the second half of the year," he added.

LME ring dealer Rudolf Wolff's director of business development, David Waite, agreed oversupply will arrive in the second half of 1997, dampening price swings and pushing the market into contango when nearby months are at a discount to prices further forward.
Not so, according to Dan Roling of Merrill Lynch, who is confident that his forecast of a balanced rather than oversupplied market will prove right for the second year running in 1997.

"We continue to maintain that demand is the issue, not supply," Roling said. "Demand, which has turned out to be much stronger than the consensus view this year, will turn out once again to be surprisingly strong next year."

Everen Securities' Vahid Fathi, who expects strong demand in China and the U.S. to bolster copper, agreed: "Almost everyone has their figures right on the supply side, but demand is understated. I see only a slight surplus in 1997."
As always the industrial metal's health will be linked to the economy's performance.

Prudential Securities noted a consensus pointing slower growth in the emerging markets. "However, the International Monetary Fund have predicted that global growth will increase from 3.8 percent this year to 4.1 percent in 1997," Prudential said.

And Everen's Fathi said North American copper producers will earn good money next year after the Sumitomo knocks in 1996. "Earnings on an operating basis will surpass 1996 because of more volume of production and cost-containment."
CRU's Lesemann added,"It should be another good profit year for the producers."
Sumitomo's woes highlighted the ferocity of delta-hedging and other arcane options-trading terms. Many producers had bought options from banks to guard against falling prices.
The banks had to cough up heavily when tags plunged on news of the Japanese trader's multi-billion dollar losses.
"I think probably the banks who got severely burned from granting out of the money options to producers, will be a lot more cautious in future," Waite said.
"Copper prices are a good deal lower so it is not as attractive for producers to hedge - that's why the volume of new options will be down," Waite said.
